plans.title: Correction Isn't Rejection
plans.subject: Series: The Coachable Athlete. A five-day performance plan that helps athletes receive feedback, separate correction from rejection, respond with maturity, and turn coaching into growth.
steps:
Mental Model

Your Talent Gets You Noticed. Your Coachability Determines What Happens Next.

Opening

There are a lot of things coaches can't give you.

They can't give you height.

They can't give you speed.

They can't give you natural ability.

But there is one thing every athlete has complete control over:

How coachable you are.

Being coachable means you can receive information, make an adjustment, and become better because of it.

And that might be one of the most underrated advantages in sports.

Because eventually, talent isn't enough.

The Story

Kobe Wanted to Be Coached

Kobe Bryant became one of the greatest basketball players of his generation.

But one of the things that separated Kobe wasn't just his ability.

He wanted information.

He studied the game. He asked questions. He learned from coaches, veteran players, and some of the greatest basketball minds he could find.

If someone knew something that could make him better, Kobe wanted to know.

Think about that.

This was one of the most confident players to ever step onto a basketball court.

But confidence didn't make Kobe think:

“Nobody can tell me anything.”

His confidence allowed him to think:

“If you know something that can make me better, tell me.”

Kobe understood something every athlete eventually has to learn:

Correction isn't an attack on who you are.

It's information about who you could become.

Why This Matters

Imagine two athletes.

They're equally talented.

They make the same mistake.

Coach corrects both of them.

The first athlete immediately gets defensive.

“I know.”

“That wasn't my fault.”

“Why are you always yelling at me?”

Their face changes.

Their body language changes.

They start explaining what happened.

They're hearing the coach's words, but they're so busy defending themselves that they're no longer listening.

The second athlete might not like the correction either.

Maybe the coach's tone bothers them.

Maybe they're embarrassed because everyone heard it.

Maybe they don't completely agree.

But instead of immediately reacting, they ask:

“What can I take from this?”

Then they make the adjustment.

Same talent.

Same mistake.

Same coaching.

Different response.

Repeat that hundreds of times over a season and those two athletes won't remain the same player.

One keeps collecting defenses.

The other keeps collecting adjustments.

And adjustments compound.

Mirror Check

“Coach Doesn't Like Me”

Now we need to talk about one of the most dangerous stories an athlete can start telling themselves.

“Coach doesn't like me.”

Maybe you've thought it before.

Coach seems harder on you than everyone else.

You get pulled after making a mistake.

Someone else makes the same mistake and stays in.

Coach barely talks to you one day.

You're not starting.

Your playing time decreases.

Coach raises their voice at you.

And slowly your mind starts putting the pieces together:

“Coach has something against me.”

“Coach doesn't believe in me.”

“Coach likes them more than me.”

“Nothing I do is good enough.”

Maybe that's true.

But here's the problem:

You don't actually know that yet.

And there's a huge difference between what happened and the story you created about what happened.

Pull Back the Curtain

Facts vs. Stories

Let's say you make two mistakes and Coach takes you out of the game.

FACT:

Coach took me out.

STORY:

Coach doesn't trust me.

You don't start.

FACT:

I'm not starting today.

STORY:

Coach doesn't believe in me.

Coach gets on you harder than a teammate.

FACT:

Coach corrected me aggressively.

STORY:

Coach likes them more than me.

See the difference?

Facts describe what happened.

Stories explain what we think it means.

And your mind can create a story so quickly that you start treating it like a fact.

That's when things can get dangerous.

Because once you believe...

“Coach doesn't like me,”

you start looking for evidence.

Coach walks past you?

See.

Coach corrects you?

See.

Coach starts someone else?

I knew it.

Coach doesn't compliment you?

Exactly.

Now everything gets filtered through the story you've already decided is true.

And eventually...

You stop responding to your coach.

You start responding to the story in your head.

The Turning Point

The athlete thinks:

“Coach doesn't like me.”

So their body language changes.

They stop asking questions.

They become defensive when they're corrected.

Their effort might drop.

They complain to teammates.

They tell their parents what Coach is doing.

They start thinking about leaving the team.

And worst of all...

They become harder to coach.

Now Coach sees an athlete with poor body language, resistance to feedback, and a bad attitude.

Which may lead to fewer opportunities.

The athlete sees the fewer opportunities and thinks:

“See! I told you Coach didn't like me.”

And the cycle continues.

The original thought starts creating the very situation the athlete was afraid of.

Deeper Look

Correction Isn't Rejection

You need to learn something that will help you far beyond sports:

Someone correcting your behavior is not necessarily rejecting you as a person.

Coach can dislike what you just did...

without disliking you.

Coach can be disappointed in your effort...

without being disappointed in who you are.

Coach can decide another athlete gives the team a better chance today...

without believing you'll never become a great player.

Those things can exist at the same time.

Mature athletes learn to separate them.

Instead of asking:

“Does Coach like me?”

Start asking:

“What is Coach trying to get out of me?”

That's a much more powerful question.

Because one question makes you search for approval.

The other makes you search for growth.

Why This Matters

Coachable Doesn't Mean Weak

There's another side of this conversation we can't ignore.

Being coachable does not mean blindly agreeing with everything a coach says.

Coaches are human.

They can make mistakes.

They can misunderstand situations.

They can communicate poorly.

And being coachable doesn't mean accepting behavior that is abusive, degrading, discriminatory, threatening, or inappropriate. If something genuinely crosses that line, talk to a parent, guardian, athletic administrator, or another trusted adult.

But there's a major difference between inappropriate behavior and:

Being challenged.

Being corrected.

Being held accountable.

Getting benched.

Being told you aren't doing enough.

Hearing something you don't want to hear.

Those things are part of competitive sports.

You don't have to love every message.

And you definitely won't love every delivery.

But a Complete Athlete learns to ask:

“Is there something inside this that can make me better?”

If there is...

Take it.

Key Takeaway

Every time you're corrected, you're being given information.

You decide what happens to it.

You can defend yourself.

You can take it personally.

You can create a story.

You can blame the coach.

Or...

You can use it.

Because the goal isn't to become an athlete who never gets corrected.

That's impossible.

The goal is to become an athlete who gets better every time they are.

Today's Challenge

Think about the last time a coach corrected you and you didn't like it.

Maybe they yelled.

Maybe you got benched.

Maybe you felt embarrassed.

Maybe you thought they were wrong.

Write down two things:

1. THE FACT

What actually happened?

Only write what you know to be true.

2. THE STORY

What did you tell yourself it meant?

Coach doesn't like me.

Coach doesn't believe in me.

Coach is playing favorites.

I'm not good enough.

Coach is always picking on me.

Now look at the two.

Are they actually the same thing?

That's the work today.

Start separating what happened from what you decided it meant.

Because you can't always control how you're coached.

But you can control what happens inside your mind after the coaching happens.

And that's where becoming coachable begins.

Complete Athlete Principle

Correction isn't rejection.

Don't let the story in your head keep you from hearing the coaching that could make you better.

plans.title: Find the Coaching
plans.subject: Series: The Coachable Athlete. A five-day performance plan that helps athletes receive feedback, separate correction from rejection, respond with maturity, and turn coaching into growth.
steps:
Mental Model

You Don't Have to Like the Delivery to Use the Message.

Opening

Let's be real.

Sometimes coaching doesn't sound nice.

It might come calmly:

“Next time, keep your head up. You had a teammate open.”

But sometimes it sounds like:

“GET YOUR HEAD UP! YOU'VE GOT TO SEE THAT!”

Same correction.

Very different delivery.

And when the delivery is tough, something happens fast.

You stop thinking about what Coach said...

and start thinking about how Coach said it.

Why did they yell at me like that?

They didn't yell at him when he did it.

Coach embarrassed me.

I know what I'm doing.

They didn't have to say it like that.

And maybe you're right.

Maybe Coach could have communicated it better.

But here's the question:

Are you going to let a delivery you didn't like make you miss information you needed?

That's where coachability becomes a competitive advantage.

Pull Back the Curtain

The Two Messages

Whenever you're coached, there can be two messages happening at the same time.

There's the emotional message you feel:

“Coach is mad at me.”

And there's the performance message you need:

“I need to make that adjustment.”

The emotional message is usually louder.

That's why athletes miss the coaching.

Imagine Coach yells:

“HOW MANY TIMES DO I HAVE TO TELL YOU? GET BACK ON DEFENSE!”

Your emotions hear:

Coach is embarrassing me.

Coach is always on me.

Why are they yelling?

But underneath all of that is a piece of information:

Get back on defense faster.

That's the coaching.

Everything else might be uncomfortable...

but that's the part that can make you better.

Your job is to find it.

System Update

C.A.R. — Catch. Ask. Respond.

When emotions start taking over, remember three words:

CATCH. ASK. RESPOND.

This is your reset when coaching gets tough.

• CATCH

Catch the emotional reaction before it controls your response.

Coach corrects you.

Immediately you feel something.

Anger.

Embarrassment.

Frustration.

Disappointment.

You might want to roll your eyes.

Shake your head.

Throw your hands up.

Explain yourself.

Say:

“I KNOW!”

Or give Coach that look that says everything without saying anything.

That's the moment.

Catch it.

You don't have to pretend you aren't frustrated.

You're allowed to feel it.

The goal isn't:

“Don't have emotions.”

The goal is:

“Don't let the emotion choose what you do next.”

One breath.

Eyes on Coach.

Listen.

Catch yourself before the reaction becomes the response.

• ASK

Now ask yourself one question:

“What's the coaching?”

Not:

Why are they yelling?

Not:

Why didn't they say that to someone else?

Not:

Why are they always on me?

Not even:

Do I agree?

First ask:

“What's the coaching?”

Strip away the volume.

Strip away the tone.

Strip away the embarrassment.

Find the information.

Coach says:

“STOP SWINGING AT PITCHES UP!”

What's the coaching?

Improve my pitch selection.

Coach says:

“YOU'RE STANDING AROUND! MOVE WITHOUT THE BALL!”

What's the coaching?

I need to create movement when I don't have the ball.

Coach says:

“YOU CAN'T TAKE THAT PLAY OFF!”

What's the coaching?

My effort dropped.

Coach says:

“YOU'RE TOO HIGH! GET YOUR PAD LEVEL DOWN!”

What's the coaching?

Fix my technique.

Different sports.

Same skill.

Find the coaching.

• RESPOND

Now comes the part that separates coachable athletes.

Make the adjustment.

Not:

“But Coach...”

Not:

“That's not what happened.”

Not:

“I already knew that.”

Not a head shake.

Not bad body language.

You can simply say:

“Got it.”

“Yes, Coach.”

Or ask a useful question if you genuinely don't understand.

Then...

Show them you heard them.

If Coach tells you to communicate more...

communicate.

If Coach tells you to sprint back...

sprint back.

If Coach corrects your technique...

attempt the correction.

Because there is a massive difference between an athlete who says:

“I understand.”

and an athlete whose next rep says:

“I understand.”

Why This Matters

Your Next Rep Is Your Response

This is one of the most powerful habits you can develop.

When Coach corrects you...

Don't spend the next five minutes thinking about the correction.

Attack the next rep.

Coach tells you to move your feet?

Next rep — move them.

Coach tells you to communicate?

Next rep — be the loudest communicator.

Coach tells you your effort isn't good enough?

Next rep — change the effort.

Your response doesn't need to be a speech.

Let your next rep speak for you.

That's coachability.

Mirror Check

But What If Coach Is Wrong?

This is where maturity matters.

Sometimes...

Coach might be wrong.

Coaches are human too.

Maybe they didn't see what happened.

Maybe another player made the mistake.

Maybe you were doing exactly what another coach told you to do.

Your first instinct might be to immediately prove your point.

But ask yourself:

“Does this need to be solved right now?”

In the middle of competition or practice, the answer is often no.

Listen.

Keep competing.

Then find the right moment to ask.

Instead of:

“That wasn't my fault!”

Try:

“Coach, can I ask you about that last play? I want to make sure I understand what you wanted me to do.”

Notice the difference.

You're not afraid to speak up.

You're not blindly agreeing.

You're seeking clarity instead of starting a fight.

That's maturity.

Deeper Look

Tough Coaching

There will probably be coaches in your athletic career who challenge you differently.

Some are calm.

Some are intense.

Some explain everything.

Some expect you to figure things out quickly.

Some will put their arm around you.

Some will get in your face.

You won't connect perfectly with every coaching style.

And that's okay.

Part of becoming a Complete Athlete is learning how to perform without needing every environment to be perfectly comfortable.

Because eventually you'll have teachers, bosses, trainers, teammates, and leaders who communicate differently too.

You don't need every messenger to communicate exactly how you prefer in order to learn from the message.

That's a skill that goes far beyond sports.

Today's Challenge

Today, we're going to practice C.A.R.

The next time you're corrected:

CATCH

What emotion showed up?

Anger? Embarrassment? Frustration?

Recognize it before reacting.

ASK

What's the coaching?

Write the actual instruction in one sentence.

RESPOND

What adjustment will you make on your next opportunity?

Then do it.

After practice or competition, come back and write:

What Coach Said:

What I Initially Felt:

The Coaching Inside the Message:

My Adjustment:

The goal isn't to become emotionless.

The goal is to become an athlete whose emotions don't block information that can make them better.

Complete Athlete Principle

Don't fight the correction. Find the coaching.

You don't have to love every delivery.

You don't have to agree with everything immediately.

But before you reject the message because you didn't like the messenger...

find the coaching.

Then let your next rep show what you did with it.

plans.title: Never Outgrow Coaching
plans.subject: Series: The Coachable Athlete. A five-day performance plan that helps athletes receive feedback, separate correction from rejection, respond with maturity, and turn coaching into growth.
steps:
Mental Model

Being Good Can Become Dangerous.

Opening

You start getting good.

You're starting. You're producing. People know what you can do.

And slowly, something can happen.

Coach corrects you:

“I know.”

Coach wants you to change something:

“What I'm doing is working.”

Coach points out a mistake after a great game:

“I just played great. What more do you want?”

Be careful.

Sometimes the hardest athlete to coach isn't the athlete who's struggling.

It's the talented athlete who starts believing their success means they don't need coaching.

The Story

Brady Never Stopped Learning

Tom Brady entered the NFL as the 199th pick in the 2000 NFL Draft.

He eventually became one of the most accomplished quarterbacks ever.

But even after the championships, records, and MVPs, the details still mattered.

Footwork.

Reads.

Timing.

Mechanics.

Decision-making.

There was always something to improve.

Imagine accomplishing that much and still being willing to hear:

“Your footwork wasn't good enough there.”

“You missed that read.”

“Your timing was off.”

That's coachability.

Success doesn't graduate you from coaching.

In fact, the better you become, the smaller the details that separate you from the next level.

Why This Matters

When You're Already Playing Well

You have a great game.

Then Coach says:

“Good game, but...”

Your first reaction might be:

Can I enjoy this for five minutes?

Yes.

Celebrate the win.

But then listen.

Coach isn't necessarily saying you played badly.

They're showing you where good could have been better.

Great athletes don't need something to go wrong before looking for improvement.

Mirror Check

When What You're Doing Is Working

Maybe Coach wants to change something that already works.

Your technique.

Your approach.

Your positioning.

Your preparation.

You think:

“Why would I change it?”

Maybe you shouldn't.

But get curious before getting defensive.

What works at your current level might not work at the next one.

Your athletic ability might even be covering up a weakness that hasn't been exposed yet.

Ask:

“Coach, can you help me understand what you're seeing?”

Deeper Look

When Someone Else Corrects You

Sometimes the useful information doesn't even come from your head coach.

An assistant coach.

A trainer.

A teammate.

Maybe even someone who wasn't as talented as you.

Your ego asks:

“What can they teach me?”

A better question is:

“Is there something here I can learn?”

You don't have to accept every opinion.

But don't become so defensive that useful information can't reach you.

The Turning Point

Don't Let Praise Make You Deaf

The better you become, the more praise you'll hear.

Parents.

Teammates.

Fans.

Social media.

Recruiters.

Enjoy it.

You've earned some of it.

But don't become addicted to voices that only tell you how good you are.

Because sometimes the person saying:

“This still needs work.”

is giving you something the praise can't.

Don't let praise make you deaf to correction.

Practice Install

Go Looking for Feedback

Don't just tolerate coaching.

Seek it.

After a good game:

“Coach, what could I have done better?”

During practice:

“Can you watch this rep and tell me what you see?”

And here's one of the best questions a talented athlete can ask:

“What's something in my game that could hurt me at the next level?”

Now you're trying to find the weakness before your competition does.

That's different.

Today's Challenge

Ask your coach:

“What's one thing in my game I need to improve, even though it hasn't hurt me yet?”

Then write down:

WHAT DID COACH SEE?

WHY DOES IT MATTER?

WHAT WILL I DO ABOUT IT?

Then attack it.

Because asking for feedback doesn't make you coachable.

What you do with the feedback does.

Complete Athlete Principle

Never become too good to be coached.

Be confident.

Celebrate your success.

Know what you're good at.

But never let success convince you that you've arrived.

The athlete who stays hungry for correction stays capable of becoming more.

plans.title: Your Response Is Speaking
plans.subject: Series: The Coachable Athlete. A five-day performance plan that helps athletes receive feedback, separate correction from rejection, respond with maturity, and turn coaching into growth.
steps:
Mental Model

Coachability Is Something People Can See.

Opening

You don't have to say:

“I don't want to hear this.”

Your body can say it for you.

Coach corrects you.

You look away.

Drop your shoulders.

Shake your head.

Roll your eyes.

Walk back slowly.

Give a half-hearted:

“Okay...”

You might think:

I didn't say anything disrespectful.

Maybe not.

But you still communicated.

The Turning Point

The Moment After the Mistake

Picture this.

You make a mistake in a big moment.

You already know you messed up.

You're frustrated with yourself.

Then Coach corrects you.

And you're thinking:

“I KNOW! You don't have to tell me!”

That's one of the hardest moments to remain coachable.

Because you're not only dealing with Coach.

You're dealing with your own frustration too.

But here's the problem:

Coach can't see everything happening inside your head.

They can only see your response.

That's why your response matters.

Mirror Check

Don't Explain Everything

One habit can quietly destroy coachability:

Having an explanation for every mistake.

Coach says:

“You were late.”

“Well, I thought...”

Coach says:

“Your effort dropped.”

“I was tired because...”

Coach says:

“You missed your assignment.”

“But they were supposed to...”

Sometimes your explanation might even be correct.

But if your first response to every correction is explaining why it wasn't really your fault, eventually people stop feeling like they can coach you.

Not every correction needs a courtroom defense.

Sometimes the most powerful response is:

“Got it. I'll fix it.”

Then fix it.

Why This Matters

Your Next Rep Tells the Truth

Anyone can say:

“Yes, Coach.”

The real test comes next.

Did you change anything?

Coach says communicate more?

Communicate.

Coach says sprint through the play?

Sprint.

Coach corrects your technique?

Try the adjustment.

Coach tells you to reset after mistakes?

Reset.

Because the best response to coaching isn't:

“I heard you.”

It's:

“Watch this.”

Your next rep should show that you listened.

Deeper Look

When You're Frustrated

You won't always handle this perfectly.

There will be moments when you're angry.

Embarrassed.

Disappointed.

That's normal.

Coachability doesn't mean you never feel those things.

It means those feelings don't get to control your behavior.

Remember what you've learned:

CATCH the emotion.

ASK what's the coaching?

RESPOND with the adjustment.

That's how you stay in control.

Today's Challenge

At your next practice or competition, pay attention to the five seconds after you're corrected.

Ask yourself:

What did my body language say?

Did I listen or immediately defend myself?

Did my next rep show an adjustment?

Then rate yourself:

COACHABILITY CHECK

Eyes: ___

Listen: ___

Acknowledge: ___

Reset: ___

Respond: ___

You don't have to be perfect.

Just become more aware.

Because eventually, the way you respond to coaching becomes part of your reputation.

Complete Athlete Principle

Your response is speaking before you ever say a word.

Great athletes don't just say they're coachable.

You can see it in what they do next.

plans.title: Control What You Can Control
plans.subject: Series: The Coachable Athlete. A five-day performance plan that helps athletes receive feedback, separate correction from rejection, respond with maturity, and turn coaching into growth.
steps:
Mental Model

You Can't Control Your Coach. You Can Control the Athlete They Have to Coach.

Opening

Every athlete will eventually have a coach they don't completely understand.

You might not like their personality.

Their communication style.

Their decisions.

How much they praise you.

How hard they push you.

And sometimes you may genuinely disagree with them.

But here's the question:

Who are you going to become because of it?

Because you can't control your coach.

But you can control the athlete you bring to them every day.

The Story

Phil Jackson Challenged Michael Jordan

When Phil Jackson became head coach of the Chicago Bulls, Michael Jordan was already one of the greatest individual players in basketball.

Jordan could score.

He could dominate games.

He could take over when his team needed him.

Then Jackson and his staff asked him to do something difficult:

Trust the system. Trust your teammates. Give up some control.

The Bulls implemented the triangle offense, which required movement, reads, passing, and involvement from the entire team.

For Jordan, that meant the answer couldn't always be:

“Give me the ball and get out of the way.”

Think about how difficult that can be for a great athlete.

What you're doing already works.

You're the superstar.

Then Coach asks you to change.

Jordan could have decided:

“Coach doesn't understand me.”

“I'm the reason we're winning.”

“Just let me play my game.”

Instead, he adapted.

He was still Michael Jordan.

Still aggressive.

Still confident.

Still capable of taking over games.

But he learned to operate within something bigger than himself.

And the Bulls eventually became a dynasty.

Sometimes coaching isn't trying to take away what makes you great.

It's trying to teach you how to use your greatness differently.

Why This Matters

You Don't Have to Agree with Everything

Coachability doesn't mean becoming a robot.

You can disagree.

You can ask questions.

You can have an opinion.

You can even believe Coach made the wrong decision.

But after all of that...

You still have to decide who you're going to be.

Will disagreement change your effort?

Will frustration change your preparation?

Will a decision you don't like change your attitude?

Will:

“Coach doesn't like me”

become permission to stop doing your job?

That's where ownership begins.

Pull Back the Curtain

Control Your Side

You cannot control:

Coach's personality.

Coach's decisions.

Coach's tone.

Who Coach praises.

How Coach sees every situation.

But you can control:

Your effort.

Your preparation.

Your attitude.

Your body language.

Your communication.

Your response to correction.

Your willingness to improve.

Spend more energy on that list.

Key Takeaway

The Complete Athlete Standard

Over the last five days, you've learned that being coachable isn't about being quiet and doing whatever you're told.

It's about maturity.

You learned:

Correction isn't rejection.

Find the coaching inside the criticism.

Never become too good to be coached.

Your response and body language matter.

And finally:

Control what you can control.

You will have great coaches.

Tough coaches.

Coaches you connect with.

And coaches you don't.

Don't require the perfect coach in order to become the athlete you're capable of becoming.

Today's Challenge

Create two columns.

OUT OF MY CONTROL

Write down everything about your current coaching situation you cannot control.

Then:

IN MY CONTROL

Write down what you can do regardless.

Circle three things from the second list.

Those become your standard.

Not when Coach praises you.

Not when everything is going your way.

Every day.

Closing the Plan

Being coachable doesn't make you less confident.

It doesn't make you weak.

And it doesn't mean someone else gets to determine who you are.

It's actually the opposite.

Coachability means your ego doesn't get in the way of your growth.

Listen.

Ask questions.

Take what can make you better.

Make the adjustment.

And keep becoming.

Because your coach may give you the correction...

but what you become because of it is up to you.

Final Complete Athlete Principle

You can't control every coach you get.

You can control the athlete every coach gets.
